readings.title: The Naughty Doll
readings.challenge: Work out who is speaking: a little girl playing mother to her doll.
readings.focus: A child copies grown-up talk about marriage, and the joke is how serious she sounds.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A girl tells us about her doll, Miss Amandy, whom she wants to marry the china vase on the mantel, the shelf above the fireplace. Dresden is a famous kind of fine china. Some old words: “forsooth” means truly; a spinster is a woman who never marries; beaux are boyfriends; to acquiesce is to agree; a suitor is someone who wants to marry. Taffy is a chewy sweet.

excerpt.locator: “The Naughty Doll,” the whole poem; opens “My dolly is a dreadful care,— Her name is Miss Amandy; I dress her up and curl her hair,…”; closes “…pretty as this vase is,— Oh, how we’ll hate the noisy men With whiskers on their faces!”.

questions.prompt: Who is the “devoted mother” in this poem, and who is her naughty child?
facilitatorNotes: The girl is the mother and her doll, Miss Amandy, is the child. She is playing at being a grown-up.
evidence: Her name is Miss Amandy;
Of her devoted mother,

questions.prompt: Whom does the girl want Amandy to marry, and whom does Amandy love?
facilitatorNotes: The china vase, a pinkish Dresden “youth”; but Amandy loves the drum. Let the child say which toy they would choose.
evidence: I’d have her wed the china vase,—
She loves the drum—that’s very plain—

questions.prompt: The girl says the drum’s promises are “hollow.” Why is that a funny word to use about a drum?
facilitatorNotes: Hollow promises are empty ones, and a drum really is hollow inside. Some children will take Amandy’s side: a noisy drum is more fun than a vase.
evidence: The protestations of the drum I am convinced are hollow;

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the girl says what she will do when she is grown up. Do you believe her?
facilitatorNotes: She promises to wait for her mama’s choice and to hate noisy men with whiskers, the opposite of Amandy. She sounds like a grown-up and a small child at once. Some children will predict she will turn out just like her doll.
evidence: I sha’n’t encourage beaux at all
Oh, how we’ll hate the noisy men With whiskers on their faces!

readings.title: Nightfall in Dordrecht
readings.challenge: Listen for the line that ends every stanza, and who sings it each time.
readings.focus: Everything in a little Dutch town, even a creaking windmill, seems to sing a child to sleep.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Dordrecht is an old town in Holland, a country of windmills, tulips and fishing boats. A windmill’s big wings are called sails. Some words: reefed means rolled up; kine are cows; a mart is a market; brine is salty water for keeping fish. The Dream-One is the poet’s name for a kind spirit who brings sleep.

excerpt.locator: “Nightfall in Dordrecht,” the whole poem; opens “The mill goes toiling slowly around With steady and solemn creak, And my little one hears…”; closes “…Dream-One sweep, And rocking your cradle she softly sings: “Sleep, little tulip, sleep!””.

questions.prompt: What does the child hear the old mill sing? What does the mill call the child?
facilitatorNotes: “Sleep, little tulip, sleep!” The child is a little tulip, the flower Holland is famous for.
evidence: My little one hears that the old mill sings:
Sleep, little tulip, sleep!

questions.prompt: The mill’s wings creep “Grimly and ghostlike.” Is the mill scary or kind? Find words for both.
facilitatorNotes: Both: a “kindly sound” and a “steady and solemn creak,” but also grim and ghostlike in the dark. The child hears the kind side. Some children may find it spooky; that is in the words too.
evidence: And my little one hears in the kindly sound
Grimly and ghostlike creep,

questions.prompt: What jobs are planned for tomorrow? Why might a parent talk about tomorrow at bedtime?
facilitatorNotes: Old dog Fritz will pull the new milk-cart, and the child will help with the cows, sheep and herring. Something to look forward to can make it easier to stop for today.
evidence: Hitched to our new milk-cart!
But now, little tulip, sleep!

questions.prompt: What does the Dream-One do to the child’s eyes? What picture does that make?
facilitatorNotes: She comes “to button the eyes,” as if eyelids could be buttoned shut like a coat. Ask the child to button their own eyes.
evidence: A Dream-One comes to button the eyes

readings.title: Pittypat and Tippytoe
readings.challenge: Hear a grown-up complain and love at the same time.
readings.focus: Messes, squabbles and torn clothes become proof of love.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Pittypat and Tippytoe are pet names a parent gives two small children, from the sound of their feet. Some words: “by these presents” is an old way of saying “by these signs”; an internecine spat is a squabble inside a family; duds are clothes; hose are stockings; smutched means smudged; havoc is a big mess.

excerpt.locator: “Pittypat and Tippytoe,” the whole poem; opens “All day long they come and go— Pittypat and Tippytoe; Footprints up and down the hall,…”; closes “…Just such trade-marks, if you sought; Oh, how glad I am ’tis so, Pittypat and Tippytoe!”.

questions.prompt: What signs tell the grown-up that the two children have been about?
facilitatorNotes: Footprints in the hall, toys on the floor, finger-marks on the wall, smudges on the door. Ask which signs your own house might show.
evidence: Footprints up and down the hall,
Finger-marks along the wall,

questions.prompt: What do the children ask for a dozen times a day, and why can’t the grown-up say no?
facilitatorNotes: Buttered bread, inches thick with sugar. The grown-up loves them too much to refuse, even when it is silly.
evidence: Inches thick with sugar too!
And I never can say, “No,

questions.prompt: The grown-up lists many worries. Do they sound really upset? Which words tell you?
facilitatorNotes: Partly: “Fie, for shame!” scolds, but “Many a little bump to kiss” is tender. Accept either reading if the child points to words; most of the poem is teasing complaint.
evidence: Fie, for shame! to quarrel so—
Many a little bump to kiss;

questions.prompt: At the end, the grown-up says the heart has “trade-marks” on it, like the smudges on the wall. What does that mean?
facilitatorNotes: The children have left marks of love inside the parent, just as they leave marks all over the house, and the parent is glad of both.
evidence: Just such trade-marks, if you sought;
Oh, how glad I am ’tis so,

readings.title: Little Blue Pigeon
readings.challenge: Notice which sounds in the night are gentle and which one is sad.
readings.focus: A star, a moonbeam and the sea each join the lullaby, and the mother keeps singing through the sadness.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A lullaby is a song to sing a baby to sleep. Here a mother calls her baby a little blue pigeon and the cradle a nest. Anguish is great pain or sorrow; to bemoan is to be sad about something.
readings.contentNote: One stanza hears the waves mourning “the ship that shall come no more,” a sad hint of a ship lost at sea. The poem does not explain it.

excerpt.locator: “Little Blue Pigeon,” the whole poem; opens “Sleep, little pigeon, and fold your wings— Little blue pigeon with velvet eyes; Sleep to…”; closes “…eyes; Am I not singing?—see, I am swinging— Swinging the nest where my darling lies.”.

questions.prompt: What does the mother call her baby, and what is the nest?
facilitatorNotes: A little blue pigeon; the nest is the cradle she is swinging.
evidence: Little blue pigeon with velvet eyes;
Swinging the nest where her little one lies.

questions.prompt: What does the moonbeam want to know?
facilitatorNotes: Whether the baby is sleeping and dreaming while the mother sings. The moonbeam creeps in quietly, like someone checking on a sleeping child.
evidence: Sleeping and dreaming while mother sings?

questions.prompt: Which sound in the poem is sad? How is it different from the star’s song?
facilitatorNotes: The star tinkles and calls; the waves sob, groan and moan for a ship that will not come back. Read the two stanzas in different voices.
evidence: Calling and tinkling the night along.
Bemoaning the ship that shall come no more.

questions.prompt: In the first stanza the pigeon has “velvet eyes.” In the last, “mournful eyes.” Why might the poet change that word?
facilitatorNotes: Mournful means sad. Perhaps the sea’s sadness has come into the room, or the mother sees her own sadness in her baby; either way she keeps singing. Accept other ideas tied to the change.
evidence: Little blue pigeon with mournful eyes;
Am I not singing?

readings.title: Teeny-Weeny
readings.challenge: Follow a game that slides from play into a dream.
readings.focus: A knee-ride becomes a brave night journey, told with a grown-up’s tender pride.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Teeny-Weeny is a small boy who rides a grown-up’s knee as if it were a horse. Some words: a palfrey is a gentle riding horse; “plies his lash” means waves his whip; the folk of fay are fairies; to put a host to rout is to chase away a crowd; By-low is the land of sleep.

excerpt.locator: “Teeny-Weeny,” the whole poem; opens “Every evening, after tea, Teeny-Weeny comes to me, And, astride my willing knee, Plies…”; closes “…When, with an exulting cry, Teeny-Weeny, vaulting high, Plies his lash and rides away!”.

questions.prompt: Who is the horse in this poem, and who gives the orders?
facilitatorNotes: The grown-up’s knee is the horse, and Teeny-Weeny is in charge: “He commands, and I obey!”
evidence: And, astride my willing knee,
He commands, and I obey!

questions.prompt: What does Teeny-Weeny shout, and what does he never shout? Why?
facilitatorNotes: “More!” and never “Whoa!” He loves to go fast and never wants to stop. Try a gentle knee-ride and see which word comes.
evidence: “More!” he cries, and never “Whoa!”

questions.prompt: Where does Teeny-Weeny ride when his eyes close, and who tells about it?
facilitatorNotes: To the land of By-low, where he chases off the fairies. He tells the tale himself “every night.” Ask whether the grown-up believes it, or just enjoys it.
evidence: Where the land of By-low is.
Every night he tells it so.

questions.prompt: What happened once when Teeny-Weeny went away? What does that tell you about the grown-up?
facilitatorNotes: The grown-up was very lonely and glad to have him back. The game is as much a joy for the horse as for the rider.
evidence: I was very lonely then;
Teeny-Weeny back again!

readings.title: Norse Lullaby
readings.challenge: Count the three singers and compare their songs.
readings.focus: A storm, a tree and a mother sing almost the same words, but only one song is close enough to comfort.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Norse means from the far north of Europe, a land of snow and pine forests. The storm-king is the poem’s name for the winter storm. “Yonder” means over there; “a-next” means next to.

excerpt.locator: “Norse Lullaby,” the whole poem; opens “The sky is dark and the hills are white As the storm-king speeds from the north to-night;…”; closes “…sleep, little one, sleep; Weary thou art, a-next my heart Sleep, little one, sleep.”.

questions.prompt: Who are the three singers in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: The storm-king, the mother pine singing to the vine, and the speaker singing to the child.
evidence: And this is the song the storm-king sings,
Clings at the foot of a mother pine;

questions.prompt: The storm-king and the pine sing nearly the same words. How are their songs different?
facilitatorNotes: The storm sings “gruffly” in “bitter flight”; the pine bends over the vine and promises protection. Same words, different voices: try both.
evidence: He rustles his wings and gruffly sings:
What shall you fear when I am here?

questions.prompt: Who is “the little snowflake at my breast”? Why might the poet call a child a snowflake?
facilitatorNotes: The baby being sung to. A snowflake is small, soft and white, and belongs to this winter night. Accept other reasons.
evidence: But the little snowflake at my breast

questions.prompt: Whose song does the child like best, and why do you think so?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker’s own song, sung “a-next my heart.” Closeness matters more than a grand voice. Some children may like the storm-king’s best; ask why.
evidence: Liketh the song I sing the best—
Weary thou art, a-next my heart

readings.title: The Fire-Hangbird’s Nest
readings.challenge: Hear a grown man remember being a boy, and notice how he feels about it now.
readings.focus: Years of failing to reach a nest become a happy memory, and the clever bird wins.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. The fire-hangbird is an old country name for the Baltimore oriole, an orange-and-black bird that weaves a hanging nest at the tip of a high branch. A grown man looks at the elm tree he tried to climb as a boy. Some words: a deacon is a church officer; a trophy is a prize; to covet is to want badly; a callow brood is a nest of baby birds; prudent means careful.
readings.contentNote: Boys fall and hurt themselves climbing the tree, and the poem remembers trying to take a bird’s nest; the speaker’s mother tells him it would be wicked to destroy the eggs.

excerpt.locator: “The Fire-Hangbird’s Nest,” the whole poem; opens “As I am sitting in the sun upon the porch to-day, I look with wonder at the elm that…”; closes “…youth I’m sure the best Would be of how they sought in vain the old fire-hangbird’s nest!”.

questions.prompt: What did the boys try to do, and why couldn’t they?
facilitatorNotes: Reach the nest; it hung from the “upper outer twig,” too high and too thin to climb to. Boys fell and broke legs and arms trying.
evidence: That dangled from that upper outer twig in taunting wise,
Philetus Baker broke his leg and Orrin Root his arm—

questions.prompt: What did the boy’s mother tell him about the nest?
facilitatorNotes: That it would be wicked to destroy a hangbird’s eggs. She also called on father and grandpa to say they never robbed a nest as boys; some children may doubt them.
evidence: She told me ’twould be wicked to destroy a hangbird’s eggs,

questions.prompt: The man says the elm “is not as tall as years ago it used to be.” Has the tree shrunk? Why does it look shorter?
facilitatorNotes: He has grown; places from childhood often look smaller to grown-ups. He even says so again near the end.
evidence: That elm is not as tall as years ago it used to be!

questions.prompt: The boys never got the nest. Is the man sorry? What does the last line say his best memory is?
facilitatorNotes: Not sorry: the best memory is “how they sought in vain,” the trying, not the winning. Some children may think he still wishes he had climbed it.
evidence: Would be of how they sought in vain the old fire-hangbird’s nest!

readings.title: Gold and Love for Dearie
readings.challenge: Compare three songs and listen for the words that change in the last one.
readings.focus: Trolls and a hard-working father sing of gold; the mother sings of love.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Trolls and elves are creatures from northern fairy tales who live in hills. Some words: to delve is to dig; dolorous means sad; furtive means sneaky; the burthen is the chorus of a song; stanch means strong and loyal. “Dearie” is the child.

excerpt.locator: “Gold and Love for Dearie,” the whole poem; opens “Out on the mountain over the town, All night long, all night long, The trolls go up and…”; closes “…is not of gold; But it’s “Love, love! nothing but love— Mother’s love for dearie!””.

questions.prompt: Who sings in each of the three stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: The trolls on the mountain, a father digging inside the hill, and the mother rocking the bed.
evidence: The trolls go up and the trolls go down,
Deep in the hill a father delves
Mother is rocking thy lowly bed

questions.prompt: The trolls and the father sing the same words. Do they sound the same? Is the father like the trolls?
facilitatorNotes: The trolls’ tune is “dolorous,” sad; the father sings “merrily” because he digs for his child. Some children will say wanting gold makes them alike; others that the father works out of love.
evidence: This is ever their dolorous tune:
And merrily ever this song he sings:

questions.prompt: What does the mother’s song have instead of gold? Which song does the poem seem to like best?
facilitatorNotes: Love, “nothing but love.” Coming last and different, it sounds like the answer. A child may argue that the father’s gold is love too; the poem lets us think about both.
evidence: And the burthen it beareth is not of gold;
Mother’s love for dearie!

readings.title: Croodlin’ Doo
readings.challenge: Hear a grown-up’s voice change from searching, to finding, to singing.
readings.focus: A little game of hide-and-find ends in a lullaby.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. “Croodlin’ doo” is an old Scottish pet name for a baby, like “cooing dove.” The poem is written the way someone might talk: “er” means her, “ever’where” is everywhere, “withouten” is without. The lea is a meadow; jinkin’ is darting about; to “go balow” is to go to sleep.

excerpt.locator: “Croodlin’ Doo,” the whole poem; opens “Ho, pretty bee, did you see my croodlin’ doo? Ho, little lamb, is she jinkin’ on the lea?…”; closes “…winkin’ an’ blinkin’ an’ singin’ to you, As you go balow, my wee, wee croodlin’ doo!”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the grown-up ask about the croodlin’ doo in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: A bee, a lamb and a fairy, and offers a lump of sugar and a posy as a reward. A posy is a little bunch of flowers.
evidence: Ho, pretty bee, did you see my croodlin’ doo?

questions.prompt: Where did the grown-up look? Where do you think the little one really was?
facilitatorNotes: In the cradle and everywhere. The poem never says; maybe hiding close by. Let the child guess and give a reason.
evidence: Looked in er cradle, but didn’t find you there—

questions.prompt: How has the grown-up felt all day?
facilitatorNotes: Lonesome, “kind lonesome,” without the little one.
evidence: B’en kind lonesome all er day withouten you—

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza sound different from the first?
facilitatorNotes: The first calls out “Ho!”; the last rocks slowly, “Rockaby, rockaby,” a lullaby. Read them one after the other and hear the voice grow quiet.
evidence: Rockaby, rockaby up to the star

readings.title: Fairy and Child
readings.challenge: Listen for the three ways the fairy offers to take the child to fairyland.
readings.focus: A fairy’s invitation is really a lullaby: each journey is a way of falling asleep.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A fairy is speaking to a sleepy child. Dear-My-Soul is a pet name. Fay means fairyland, and a katydid is a green insect that sings at night. Balow is an old word used in lullabies, so the “land of Balow” is the land of sleep. A halo is a ring of light, and gossamer means very thin and light, like a spider’s thread.

excerpt.locator: “Fairy and Child,” the whole poem; opens “Oh, listen, little Dear-My-Soul, To the fairy voices calling, For the moon is high in the…”; closes “…shall twinkle And dream sweet dreams as over their beams Your footfalls softly tinkle.”.

questions.prompt: Who is calling the child, and what time of night is it?
facilitatorNotes: Fairy voices, with bluebells ringing and the katydid singing; it is midnight, with the moon high.
evidence: For the moon is high in the misty sky
To the midnight feast in the clover bloom

questions.prompt: What are the ways the child could travel to fairyland?
facilitatorNotes: Walking hand in hand, sailing in a lily leaf over a stream of mist, or flying and dancing with gossamer wings.
evidence: Or we’ll sail along in a lily leaf
Two gossamer wings and airy,

questions.prompt: The second stanza begins, “Oh, slumber.” What is the fairy really asking the child to do?
facilitatorNotes: To go to sleep. The journey to the land of Balow is a dream; some children will say the fairy really takes the child. Both can be held at once.
evidence: Oh, slumber, little Dear-My-Soul,

questions.prompt: The moon smiles and thinks the child is a little fairy. Which picture in the poem do you like best, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Any picture, with its words: the lily-leaf boat, the dancing in the velvet sky, the twinkling stars.
evidence: And think you a little fairy;

readings.title: Ganderfeather’s Gift
readings.challenge: Listen for all the fairies’ names, and find out what Ganderfeather left behind.
readings.focus: A grown-up turns a mole on his cheek into a fairy’s kiss and a lifelong friend.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A grown man remembers a night when he was small. Boons are gifts. A trundle-bed is a low bed for a child. Heather is a low shrubby plant on wild hills. A sprite is a fairy; attenuate means thin, and buxom here means plump. A mole is a small dark spot on the skin that some people are born with; mayhap means perhaps. Prankish means fond of tricks.

excerpt.locator: “Ganderfeather’s Gift,” the whole poem; opens “I was just a little thing When a fairy came and kissed me; Floating in upon the light Of…”; closes “…friends this mole and I, Who have been so long together. Thank you, little Ganderfeather!”.

questions.prompt: Name as many of the fairies as you can. Which name do you like best?
facilitatorNotes: Simmerdew, Daisybright, Turtledove, Pilfercurds, Honeylove, Thistleblow, Amberglee and Ganderfeather. Pilfercurds might steal curds: ask what a name tells you.
evidence: Pilfercurds and Honeylove,

questions.prompt: What does Ganderfeather look like? Is he a thin, floaty fairy?
facilitatorNotes: No: he is plump, quaint and merry, not thin.
evidence: No attenuate sprite was he,
—But as buxom as could be;—

questions.prompt: What is the gift Ganderfeather brought?
facilitatorNotes: A mole on his cheek, which the man calls the kiss-mark of the fairy.
evidence: On my cheek uprose a berry
But the kiss-mark of that chap

questions.prompt: Why might a grown-up tell this story about a mole on his face?
facilitatorNotes: It makes something ordinary, perhaps something he once disliked, into something special. Some children will think he believes it; others that he is playing. Ask what in the last stanza shows how he feels.
evidence: Constant friends this mole and I,
Thank you, little Ganderfeather!

readings.title: “Booh!”
readings.challenge: Notice who is telling this poem, and how the baby’s feelings about the game change.
readings.focus: A father’s peekaboo game frightens his baby at first and then becomes their favourite fun.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A father is speaking about his baby son. “Booh!” is how Field spells “boo!” A monarch is a king, and despotic means bossy, like a king who must be obeyed. “Do it all aden” is the baby’s way of saying “again.” A progenitor is a parent. To rue is to be sorry about something.

excerpt.locator: “Booh!,” the whole poem; opens “On afternoons, when baby boy has had a splendid nap, And sits, like any monarch on his…”; closes “…I am sure that we shall rue The time when we are both too old to play the game of “Booh!””.

questions.prompt: How does the father play the game? Act it out with a handkerchief or your hands.
facilitatorNotes: He hides his face, moves quietly about, then suddenly shows his face and says “Booh!”
evidence: Then, with a cry, I suddenly expose my face to view,

questions.prompt: What did the baby do when the father first began? What does he do now?
facilitatorNotes: At first he stared and his lip came out as if to cry, and mamma and the nurse called it a cruel shame; now he laughs and kicks his heels. He learned that the game is fun.
evidence: And then his under lip came out and farther out it came,
But laugh and kick his little heels when I say “Booh!”

questions.prompt: The father calls the baby a king on a throne. What order does the baby give him?
facilitatorNotes: “Do it all aden!” A tiny baby bosses his father, and the father happily obeys. Ask why that is funny.
evidence: In shrill, despotic treble bids me “do it all aden!”

questions.prompt: Why does the father say they will be sorry when they are “both too old” for the game? Who is having more fun?
facilitatorNotes: He knows the baby will grow up and the game will end, so he treasures it now. Many children will say both are having fun; some will say the father, who calls it “oh, such fun!”
evidence: The time when we are both too old to play the game of “Booh!”

readings.title: The Night Wind
readings.challenge: Make the wind’s sound with me every time it comes.
readings.focus: A grown-up remembers being told the night wind howls about naughty children, and passes the joke on.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. To brood is to hang over something heavily; to wail is to cry long and loud. A tad is a small child. Ruefulest means saddest, most sorry. A “model” child is a perfectly good one.

excerpt.locator: “The Night Wind,” the whole poem; opens “Have you ever heard the wind go “Yooooo”? ’Tis a pitiful sound to hear! It seems to chill…”; closes “…true; For the wind will moan in its ruefulest tone: “Yoooooooo! Yoooooooo! Yoooooooo!””.

questions.prompt: What does the night wind say? Let’s say it together, long and low.
facilitatorNotes: “Yoooooooo!” three times at the end of each stanza.
evidence: Yoooooooo!

questions.prompt: What did the speaker’s mother tell him the wind meant?
facilitatorNotes: That somebody had been bad.
evidence: Somebody had been bad;

questions.prompt: Snug in bed, he wonders “what boy she meant.” Do you think he knew?
facilitatorNotes: Probably himself: he had been sent to bed. The joke is that he pretends not to know.
evidence: And wonder what boy she meant!

questions.prompt: The speaker says he is “quite a model now.” Do you believe him? Is the wind really telling who is naughty?
facilitatorNotes: He is teasing; a grown-up winking at a child. Some children will half believe the wind; let them say why. The real wind sounds the same for everyone.
evidence: Yes, though I’m quite a model now,
Suppose you ask, “Who has been bad?”

readings.title: The Duel
readings.challenge: Listen for who tells the storyteller what happened.
readings.focus: Two toys have a fight so fierce they vanish, and the storyteller swears it is true.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A duel is a fight between two. Gingham and calico are cotton cloths, so these are a cloth dog and a cloth cat, toys stuffed with rags. A Dutch clock is a wall clock; a Chinese plate is a china plate with blue pictures. A spat is a small quarrel, and a family row is a family quarrel.

excerpt.locator: “The Duel,” the whole poem; opens “The gingham dog and the calico cat Side by side on the table sat; ’Twas half-past twelve,…”; closes “…think of that! (The old Dutch clock it told me so, And that is how I came to know.)”.

questions.prompt: Who sat on the table, and who watched them?
facilitatorNotes: The gingham dog and the calico cat sat side by side; the old Dutch clock and the Chinese plate watched.
evidence: The gingham dog and the calico cat

questions.prompt: What did the clock and the plate do while the dog and cat fought?
facilitatorNotes: The clock put its hands over its face; the plate looked blue and wailed.
evidence: Up with its hands before its face,
And wailed, “Oh, dear! what shall we do!”

questions.prompt: What happened to the dog and the cat? Could it really happen?
facilitatorNotes: The poem says they ate each other up; nothing was left. It cannot happen, which is the joke.
evidence: Is this: they ate each other up!

questions.prompt: The storyteller keeps saying he wasn’t there and was only told. Why does he keep saying so?
facilitatorNotes: It makes the tall tale sound serious and true, and lets him off if we don’t believe it. Some children will say it is because the clock and plate saw everything; both are fair.
evidence: (I wasn’t there; I simply state
And that is how I came to know.)

readings.title: Good-Children Street
readings.challenge: Listen for the line that comes back, and picture each thing the children are doing.
readings.focus: A grown-up thinks of a street full of children at play, and the thought cheers him whatever happens.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Fondly means lovingly. To frolic and scamper is to play and run about. Fleet means fast. A legion is a big army, and plumes are feathers worn on hats. Asthmatic’ly shrill means squeaky and wheezy. A jubilee is a big celebration. Toil and vexation are hard work and worry, and poverty is being poor.

excerpt.locator: “Good-Children Street,” the whole poem; opens “There’s a dear little home in Good-Children street— My heart turneth fondly to-day Where…”; closes “…maketh life ever joyous and sweet: There’s a dear little home in Good-Children street.”.

questions.prompt: What toys do the children of Good-Children street play with? Find as many as you can.
facilitatorNotes: Dollies, tin tops, drums, guns painted red, swords, caps, plumes, a stick-horse and banners.
evidence: With dollies and tin tops and drums,
On a stick-horse that prances and snorts!

questions.prompt: What is wrong with Odette’s dolly? Why does the poet say she is “ill”?
facilitatorNotes: She has lost an eye and her feet, and her voice squeaks. The poet pretends a worn-out toy is a sick person, as children do in play.
evidence: For one of her blue china eyes has dropped out
she is minus her feet

questions.prompt: Which line comes back, and what does it say about the children’s days?
facilitatorNotes: “Oh, days they are golden and days they are fleet”: happy days that go by fast, until bedtime comes too soon.
evidence: Oh, days they are golden and days they are fleet

questions.prompt: The speaker is grown up and may be poor and worried. Why does thinking of Good-Children street make his life sweet?
facilitatorNotes: Thinking of a happy home full of playing children cheers him whatever his troubles. Some children will think he lived there as a boy, others that he is a father there now; the poem lets both fit.
evidence: This thought maketh life ever joyous and sweet:

readings.title: The Bottle Tree
readings.challenge: Work out who is speaking, and what the speaker wants more than anything.
readings.focus: A hungry baby dreams of a magic tree that grows bottles of milk.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Winkyway land is a dreamland Field made up. “Heigh-ho” is a happy cry, like “hooray.” To bloom is to flower, and -eth is an old ending, so “bloometh” means blooms. A berth is a bed on a ship. As much as you list means as much as you like. Colic is a baby’s tummy-ache. A repast is a meal. To expand is to get bigger, and fain means gladly.

excerpt.locator: “The Bottle Tree,” the whole poem; opens “A bottle tree bloometh in Winkyway land— Heigh-ho for a bottle, I say! A snug little…”; closes “…away, For I hunger and thirst for that precious repast— Heigh-ho for a bottle, I say!”.

questions.prompt: Who is talking in this poem? What clues tell you?
facilitatorNotes: A baby: it wants a bottle, a cradle and cuddling, and talks of colic and dimpled hands.
evidence: Heigh-ho for a bottle, I say!
And cuddle me snug in my cradle away,

questions.prompt: What is special about the Bottle Tree?
facilitatorNotes: It grows bottles of milk for fruit, by night and by day, and babies may take as many as they like with no tummy-ache.
evidence: You take of that fruit as much as you list,
A bottle of milk that is creamy and white!

questions.prompt: The baby says it would like to understand one trick of the fruit. What is the trick, and why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: The fruit makes babies’ bellies grow big. Of course they grow big from drinking all that milk; the baby has not worked out the plain answer.
evidence: Makes bellies of Bottle-Tree babies expand—

questions.prompt: Which lines come back in both stanzas? How do they sound like a baby asking?
facilitatorNotes: “So cuddle me close…” and “Heigh-ho for a bottle, I say!” They repeat the way a hungry baby keeps asking. Children may chant them together.
evidence: So cuddle me close, and cuddle me fast,

readings.title: The Bench-Legged Fyce
readings.challenge: Listen past the old country talk to picture the dog, and find the bravest thing he did.
readings.focus: A grown man remembers the funny, loyal little dog of his boyhood.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. The speaker talks the way country people in Missouri once did: “dorg” is dog, “wuz” is was, “hed” is had, “yaller” is yellow, “nary” is not one, “thar” is there, “medder” is meadow, and “vittles” are food. A fyce (say “fice”) is a small mixed-breed dog; bench-legged means with short, bowed legs. Sooner was his nickname: he would sooner sleep than anything. Chronic repose means resting all the time, and a forte is something you are good at. St. Joe is St. Joseph, a town in Missouri. A dude is a dressed-up fellow, and courting is visiting a girl one hopes to marry. To demur is to object, chaff is teasing, and valor is bravery.
readings.contentNote: The dog fights the country dogs and tears a visitor’s suit, and the children pull his fur and twist his tail; he never minds. The country speech is written as it sounded.

excerpt.locator: “The Bench-Legged Fyce,” the whole poem; opens “Speakin’ of dorgs, my bench-legged fyce Hed most o’ the virtues, an’ nary a vice. Some…”; closes “…of the loyalty, valor, an’ truth Of the friendships that hallow the season of youth!”.

questions.prompt: What did the fyce look like? Find two funny details.
facilitatorNotes: Long in the body, yellow, with a long curling tail; legs so crooked that he was as tall sitting as standing; and when he didn’t wag his tail, the tail wagged him.
evidence: When he didn’t wag it, why, the tail it wagged him!
Wuz as tall settin’ down as he wuz standin’ up!

questions.prompt: Why did some folks call him Sooner? Was he really lazy?
facilitatorNotes: He would sooner rest than anything; but when roused he could not be beaten, and he was boss of all the country dogs. Both things are true of him.
evidence: From his predisposition to chronic repose;
By common consent he wuz boss in St. Joe,

questions.prompt: How did the fyce treat the children, and what did he do when the Hobart boy fell through the ice?
facilitatorNotes: He let them pull his fur and twist his tail and seemed to laugh, and he dragged the Hobart boy ashore. Ask which matters more to the speaker, the fun or the rescue.
evidence: He wuz good to us kids
He wuz drug clean ashore by that bench-legged fyce!

questions.prompt: The speaker is old now. Why does he say every boy should have a pup?
facilitatorNotes: A dog’s friendship is one of the best memories of growing up; he still loves to think of his. Some children will talk about a pet of their own; others may say any true friend counts.
evidence: With no friendship subsistin’ ’tween him an’ a pup!

readings.title: Little Miss Brag
readings.challenge: Decide which girl is the rich one and which is the poor one, and which one wishes she were the other.
readings.focus: A poor girl brags about what she has, and the rich girl envies her.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A slip here is a light dress. Gingham is a plain cotton cloth, and faded means its colour has worn pale. To extol is to praise. Footmen are servants who ride on the outside of a rich family’s carriage; to trundle is to push along in a little cart. Treble is a high voice.

excerpt.locator: “Little Miss Brag,” the whole poem; opens “Little Miss Brag has much to say To the rich little lady from over the way, And the rich…”; closes “…Praise of the treasures all its own! So I’ve come to love that treble tone— “Aha, Oho!””.

questions.prompt: What does the rich little lady have? What does Miss Brag have?
facilitatorNotes: The rich girl has white dresses, many beautiful dolls and a carriage with footmen. Miss Brag has a faded gingham dress, a raggedy home-made doll and a moonlit attic room.
evidence: Has beautiful dolls in vast array;
Yet she envies the raggedy home-made doll

questions.prompt: Why might the raggedy doll be better than the beautiful dolls?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing can hurt it: wet, heat, tumbles or dirt. You can really play with it.
evidence: For the raggedy doll can fear no hurt

questions.prompt: What does the rich girl wish her mother and father would do?
facilitatorNotes: Push her around the park and sing to her like Miss Brag’s parents. She has servants but wishes for time with them.
evidence: Her father would trundle her in the park;—

questions.prompt: The last stanza says Miss Brag may sigh sometimes. Why does the poet love her bragging?
facilitatorNotes: She may wish for nice things too, but she praises what she has, and that is a kind of courage. Some children will say she brags too much; the poem lets us decide.
evidence: Often the bitter sighs upstart—
Praise of the treasures all its own!

readings.title: Shuffle-Shoon and Amber-Locks
readings.challenge: Work out who Shuffle-Shoon is and who Amber-Locks is from their names.
readings.focus: An old man and a little child build with blocks, one dreaming forward and one remembering.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Shoon is an old word for shoes, so Shuffle-Shoon shuffles his feet as old people may; amber is a golden colour, so Amber-Locks has golden hair. Reconciled means at peace together. Prattle is a small child’s chatter; quoth means said, and levelled means knocked flat.

excerpt.locator: “Shuffle-Shoon and Amber-Locks,” the whole poem; opens “Shuffle-Shoon and Amber-Locks Sit together, building blocks; Shuffle-Shoon is old and…”; closes “…of the By and By; Side by side, they build their blocks— Shuffle-Shoon and Amber-Locks.”.

questions.prompt: Who is Shuffle-Shoon and who is Amber-Locks? How do their names help?
facilitatorNotes: Shuffle-Shoon is old and gray and shuffles; Amber-Locks is a little child with golden hair.
evidence: Shuffle-Shoon is old and gray,

questions.prompt: What castle will the child build when he grows up?
facilitatorNotes: One with a broad gateway, a vine, a soldier guard and a tower so high folks will wonder.
evidence: And the tower shall be so high,

questions.prompt: What does the old man mean when he says the years have levelled what he built?
facilitatorNotes: He also had big plans when young, and they did not all come true; time knocked them down like blocks. Children may say he means real buildings; ask whether that fits “dead hopes.”
evidence: But the years have levelled low

questions.prompt: One talks of the Long Ago, one of the By and By. Why do they play so happily together?
facilitatorNotes: Each enjoys building; the old man enjoys the child’s hopes, and the child has a friend. Accept answers from the last stanza.
evidence: Side by side, they build their blocks—

readings.title: Little-Oh-Dear
readings.challenge: Listen for what is strange about this garden.
readings.focus: A father makes a make-believe garden for his little girl, and her love keeps it summer in his heart.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Little-Oh-Dear is a pet name for a small girl. Posies are flowers, and gaudy means very bright. Queer means odd. A trellis is a frame for plants to climb. To make obeisance is to bow, and reverent cheer is a respectful welcome. To smite is to strike: the echo strikes the father’s heart. To wither is to dry up and die.

excerpt.locator: “Little-Oh-Dear,” the whole poem; opens “See, what a wonderful garden is here, Planted and trimmed for my Little-Oh-Dear! Posies…”; closes “…oh, it is always the summer-time here With that song of “I love you,” my Little-Oh-Dear!”.

questions.prompt: What is strange about the flowers in this garden?
facilitatorNotes: Marigolds are white and buttercups blue, the grass is brown, a cactus climbs a trellis and a tree is lavender: everything is the wrong colour or in the wrong place. It may be a play garden of toys, paper or paint.
evidence: Marigolds white and buttercups blue,
Posies so gaudy and grass of such brown—

questions.prompt: What does the silver-bird sing, and who answers it?
facilitatorNotes: “I love you,” all day long, and Little-Oh-Dear echoes it back.
evidence: “I love you—I love you!” the happy day long;—

questions.prompt: The father says the garden may wither and the bird fly away. Why doesn’t he mind?
facilitatorNotes: Her love is what matters to him: she walks “in my heart,” where it is always summer. Some children will say the garden matters too, because he made it for her.
evidence: But what careth my little precious, or I?
And, oh, it is always the summer-time here

readings.title: The Doll’s Wooing
readings.challenge: Listen for the two words the French doll can say, and how they fit every part of the story.
readings.focus: A worn-out soldier doll falls in love with a talking doll who only ever says “Mamma!”
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. Some dolls of Field’s time had a squeaker inside that said “Mamma!” when pressed. Tricked out means dressed up, and tresses are long hair. Accosted means spoken to. Stockinet is a stretchy knitted cloth; frowzy and bleared mean messy and worn; regimentals are a soldier’s uniform. To woo is to court someone you hope to marry, and plaintive means sad-sounding. Feminine means like a girl or woman, masculine like a boy or man. Vouchsafed means gave. Blue-blooded means from a noble family.

excerpt.locator: “The Doll’s Wooing,” the whole poem; opens “The little French doll was a dear little doll Tricked out in the sweetest of dresses; Her…”; closes “…ago, as I journeyed that way, I’m sure that I heard a wee baby voice say: “Mamma! mamma!””.

questions.prompt: How are the two dolls different?
facilitatorNotes: She is a dear French doll in the sweetest dresses, with blue eyes and dark hair; he is a stockinet soldier with one arm and one leg in a torn yellow uniform.
evidence: Tricked out in the sweetest of dresses;
The stockinet doll, with one arm and one leg,

questions.prompt: What is the only thing the French doll ever says, and why?
facilitatorNotes: “Mamma! mamma!” She is a talking doll that says just that whenever anyone speaks to her. The poem pretends it is her good manners.
evidence: That whenever accosted her little mouth said:

questions.prompt: Who is the dolls’ “mother,” and why can she make no objection to the wedding?
facilitatorNotes: A little girl of five. The poet jokes that a stockinet doll is not “blue-blooded,” but she has no real objection; the fun is a child playing at grown-up worries.
evidence: Her mother—a sweet little lady of five—
She really could make no objection!

questions.prompt: At the end the poet hears a wee baby voice say “Mamma! mamma!” What does he want us to imagine?
facilitatorNotes: That the dolls have a baby doll of their own, which says “Mamma!” too. Some children will say it is just the French doll again; the poem lets us wonder.
evidence: I’m sure that I heard a wee baby voice say:

readings.title: Seein’ Things
readings.challenge: Listen for the line that ends every stanza, and for the times the boy sees things most.
readings.focus: A boy who says he is brave admits what frightens him at night, and why.
readings.context: From Poems of Childhood (1904) by Eugene Field, an American newspaper writer who wrote many poems for and about children. A boy talks the way he would speak: “afeard” and “skeered” mean afraid, “uv” means of, “’at” means that, and “alluz” means always. To lick someone here means to beat him in a fight. The Tempter is a name for whoever tempts you to do wrong. It is read on Halloween, a night for enjoying a scare about things that are not really there.
readings.contentNote: The boy has been in a fight, and is sent to bed without supper; he twice says girls are more easily frightened, an old idea worth questioning.

excerpt.locator: “Seein’ Things,” the whole poem; opens “I ain’t afeard uv snakes, or toads, or bugs, or worms, or mice, An’ things ’at girls are…”; closes “…wipe me slowly out o’ sight Than I should keep a-livin’ on an’ seein’ things at night!”.

questions.prompt: What does the boy say he is not afraid of? What does he hate?
facilitatorNotes: Snakes, toads, bugs, worms and mice; he hates going to bed, because he sees things at night.
evidence: I ain’t afeard uv snakes, or toads, or bugs, or worms, or mice,

questions.prompt: What are the “things” like? Where are they?
facilitatorNotes: In the corner, by the door, in the middle of the floor; creeping silently, black or white.
evidence: So softly an’ so creepylike they never make a sound!

questions.prompt: When does he see things most? What does he think makes them come?
facilitatorNotes: “Almost alluz when I’m bad,” as after the fight. He thinks being naughty brings them, though they may come from worry.
evidence: It’s almost alluz when I’m bad I see things at night!

questions.prompt: He says girls get more scared than boys, but he hides his head and holds his breath. Is he as brave as he says?
facilitatorNotes: Not quite: he is scared too. Boys and girls can both be brave and both be scared. Some children will defend him; ask for the words that show how he really feels.
evidence: Bein’ I’m a boy, I duck my head an’ hold my breath;
